analysis.one_liner: Let single companies own newspapers and broadcast stations together and control more TV stations nationwide and in the same market.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to a House committee and subcommittee in February and March 2003, drew no cosponsors, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal media ownership rules to let media companies grow much larger. It would have removed the ban on one company owning both a daily newspaper and a radio or TV station in the same market, raised the national limit on how much of the U.S. TV audience a single company may reach from 35% to 45% of households, and let one owner hold two TV stations in the same market in more circumstances. The stated aim was fewer restrictions on media ownership; the effect would have been fewer independent owners of local news and information outlets.
analysis.who_benefits: Large media companies. Newspaper publishers could buy radio and TV stations in their own markets and vice versa. National TV station groups could expand their combined reach to 45% of U.S. television households, with UHF stations counted at only half their audience. Companies could own two TV stations in the same market wherever six independent broadcast or cable voices would remain, with all of a market's cable systems counted as a single voice. Companies that own several stations could cover more of the country and more of each local market with fewer separate owners.

how_it_helps.text: It would have eliminated the rule barring one company from owning a daily newspaper and an AM or FM radio station or TV station in the same market, letting a single owner combine print and broadcast outlets [S2][S3].
It would have raised the national cap on total TV audience reach for one company from 35% to 45% of U.S. television households [S2][S3].

It would have credited UHF stations with only half the households in their market when counting that reach, making it easier for a big owner to stay under the cap while holding more stations [S2][S3].

It would have let a company own two TV stations in the same market whenever their signals did not overlap, or where at least six independent broadcast or cable TV voices would remain afterward — counting all of a market's cable as a single voice [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary viewers and readers, mainly through reduced media diversity. When one company owns the local newspaper, several radio stations, and two TV stations in the same market, fewer independent voices remain to cover local government, run competing editorials, and produce competing local newscasts. Consolidation also tends to reduce local news production in smaller markets, where companies often share one newscast across several stations they own.
analysis.who_pays_short: Viewers and readers of local news

drawbacks.text: The bill counted all of cable television in a market as a single 'independent voice' even where many cable systems exist [S3], and allowed a company to own two stations in the same market wherever six voices would remain [S2]. In practice that could leave a town where two stations, the newspaper, and the cable system all shared one or two corporate owners, thinning local news competition rather than thickening it.

Raising the national TV reach cap from 35% to 45% [S2][S3] and crediting UHF stations with only half their households [S2][S3] would let a single company reach roughly nine in ten U.S. TV households, concentrating national programming and political advertising decisions in fewer hands.

The bill stripped the FCC of discretion on several points: it required the newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership ban to be eliminated within 90 days of enactment and barred the Commission from revising the specific national-cap regulation while implementing the higher 45% limit [S3]. A good-faith defense of ownership limits holds that these judgments belong with the expert agency after a public record, not with statutory deadlines fixed in advance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would have gone almost entirely to large media companies: bigger national footprints, ownership of both the newspaper and the broadcast station in the same town, and duopolies in local TV. The costs would have been diffuse but real — fewer independent owners means fewer independent editorial voices, more replicated local newscasts, and less local accountability reporting, with the smallest markets hit first. No provision in the bill created a comparable benefit for the viewing public; its protections (a six-voice floor, the UHF discount) were modest offsets to its own loosening. The bill's death preserved the existing ownership limits for the rest of the 108th Congress at no identifiable public cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its telecommunications subcommittee, and never got a hearing or a vote, so it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Representative Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on February 27, 2003 [S1][S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced, and on March 17, 2003 to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet [S5].

No further action appears in the record: the subcommittee never reported the bill, the full House never voted on it, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large media owners hoping to expand are no better off, but neither are they worse off — the existing ownership limits simply stayed in place. The public kept the rules that cap how much of the national TV audience one company may control and bar one owner from combining the local newspaper with local broadcast stations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing ownership limits and the public they protect

for.name: Rep. Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 27, 2003 to loosen FCC media ownership limits [S1][S3][S5].

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral in the House
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral on February 27, 2003; its Telecommunications and the Internet Subcommittee likewise reported nothing, so the bill never came to a hearing or floor vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member cosponsored the bill from either party [S4], so the record shows no partisan lineup on the measure itself.

industries.note: The bill would let big TV station chains expand their national reach from 35% to 45% of TV households, get credit for only half of their UHF stations' audiences, and own two stations in the same market. Fewer independent owners generally means fewer competing local newscasts and less local accountability reporting. For ordinary viewers this runs against their interest.

Eliminating the cross-ownership ban would let newspaper publishers buy broadcast stations in their own markets — or let broadcasters buy the local paper — combining the main print and broadcast outlets under one owner. For readers and viewers this can shrink the range of independent voices covering local government.

The cross-ownership change applies to AM and FM radio as well as television, letting large radio owners add a daily newspaper in the same market. Combined with existing consolidation, this further narrows the number of independently programmed local voices.

The bill counts all of a market's cable systems as a single 'independent voice' when deciding whether a broadcaster may own a second local station [S3]. That framing helps broadcasters justify consolidation, while cable operators themselves neither gain ownership rights nor lose them directly under the bill.
